prospect.name: Andrew Kline
prospect.location: New York City — 65 East 96th Street, near Central Park — with a second home on Long Island; lifelong New Yorker, college in New Hampshire
prospect.occupation: Ran a third-generation family commercial pest control business with his father and sold it to Terminix in 2019; then Head of M&A at Terminix for a couple of years; consulted after Terminix was itself sold; then CEO of a private-equity portfolio company, a chemical manufacturer; recently stepped down to a board seat plus consulting work. Explicitly has time now — 'certainly I have time to focus on me.'
prospect.family_status: Married — a wife interrupts the call and he confirms 'Yeah. Mr. Andrew.' Has at least one son, currently doing door-to-door sales for a company Andrew helped start and invested in.
prospect.training_background: Very experienced. Former marathon runner with nine marathons, stopped because of the joint impact. Six years of self-directed kettlebell work since COVID. Trains four to six days a week, of which at least three and sometimes six are kettlebell sessions, plus two weekly high-intensity classes on skier, bike and rower, swimming at the Long Island house and jump rope. Layers 200 to 300 push-ups into every workout. Works with 20, 22 and 24 kg bells and owns 28s, 30s and 32s, with up to 34 kg at the Long Island gym. Pays roughly $100 a month for the Ladder app following coach Lauren Kansky, and trains three or four times a month with Kelvin Gary, a New York gym owner and former University of Miami tight end whom he describes as 'the smartest guy that I've met in fitness'. Has followed Trevor's free content closely for years, including walking kettlebells three quarters of a mile to Central Park.
prospect.medical: Reports no current conditions, injuries or chronic pain — asked directly and answered 'No, no issues.' Historic back problems which he says resolved once he stopped running and shifted focus to core strength. Volunteered one movement limitation: restricted shoulder mobility that prevents him doing windmills properly and caps his Turkish get-up at 12 to 14 kg per arm.

signals: Explicitly rules out the rescue framing himself: 'it's really not about sort of like weight or it's not about consistency. It's about, you know, getting to the next, you know, continuing to grow with this' and 'maybe it would be much easier if I said, I'm 15 or 20 pounds overweight, want to lose. That's my goal. I really don't.'

Already fit and already successful — nine marathons, six years of kettlebells, four to six sessions a week, and a career from family-business owner through Terminix M&A to private-equity portfolio CEO

Price registered as a non-event. '$6,000.' … 'Okay. Sound good? And that's for the six months? For the six months, yeah. Okay. That sounds good.' He later corrected the rep's attempt to characterise it as a money objection: 'It's really the last thing.'
Buying mastery rather than results: 'it is a question of mastering it', and rated the programme a 10 against a benchmark of the best coach he has ever worked with
Unusual secondary motive, volunteered twice — guilt at consuming the founder's free content: 'I sort of feel guilty that I'm sort of like taking Trevor's work for free'

goals.text: Press or snatch 26 kg double overhead for a 30-minute workout within six months — named as the specific six-month target
Break through a plateau on overhead lifting, currently stuck working at 22 to 24 kg despite owning heavier bells
Master kettlebells at the highest level he personally can, without intending to teach
Improve shoulder mobility so he can do windmills properly and progress the Turkish get-up beyond 12 to 14 kg per arm
Build more muscle as a hedge against ageing, on the basis that muscle and a strong core are linked to longevity and injury resistance
Stay injury-free as an ageing athlete
More variety and more challenge than his current app programming provides — 'I'm bored of it'
Protect the post-workout state he relies on for mental equilibrium — 'it's become a part of my sort of like sanity check'

pains.text: Plateaued on overhead work — 'every once in a while, try and bump the weight up, you know, even to 24s, and I, it's just, I'm just not getting there'
Bored with his current programming and finding it insufficiently challenging — 'the Ladder workouts are almost like too easy for me, and I feel like I'm not getting challenged'
Restricted shoulder mobility limiting windmills and Turkish get-ups, which he suspects comes from over-focusing on push-ups

Self-programming without expertise and suspecting it is the ceiling — 'I guess I could figure it out on my own. But... maybe I should be working with somebody like him in order to continue to get better'
Guilt at using the founder's free content for years without paying — raised unprompted on two separate occasions
Travel disrupts training and hotel gyms do not motivate him — 'when I'm traveling and there's a gym, then it's hard for me to sort of like motivate myself'
Feels off, though not depressed, when he cannot train — the workout is load-bearing for his mental state
Historic back problems from marathon running, which he considers resolved

objections.raw_quote: I'd love to actually take a look at that document, if that's all right, and then let me get back to you at the beginning of the week after this holiday weekend because, I mean, I wasn't prepared to sign on the bottom line today, if that's not too much trouble. But definitely am very, very interested, and this is, I think, what I would like to do.
objections.rep_response: Agreed immediately, re-checked belief in the programme, then isolated well — 'what else is coming up that we need to figure out over the weekend?' — which reduced the objection to reading the contract and exiting the Ladder subscription. He explored the Ladder contract terms and established it was month-to-month and cancellable at any time. He did not run any of the scripted deliberation moves and did not offer to walk the remaining contract clauses live despite having the document open and shared on screen.

objections.raw_quote: Amex, but I would love to see something a little bit more in writing before I give you my credit card or if that's not too much trouble.
objections.rep_response: Complied without resistance, found the coaching agreement, shared his screen and read the whole thing aloud — services, weekly live class, form feedback, direct text access, app features, the $500 performance reward credit and the full performance guarantee with its eligibility conditions. Then texted the document over at the end of the call.

objections.raw_quote: he puts up enough variety that, again, I could just draft off of him and pick and choose and, you know, forever. And maybe that's what we'll end up doing.
objections.rep_response: Not addressed. The prospect stated plainly that continuing to use the free content indefinitely was a live option and the rep did not respond to it at all, moving on to the Central Park kettlebell walks. It never resurfaced.

objections.raw_quote: I got to get out of my ladder contract. I got to, you know, so, so I want to do. I want to take a look at it. want to see what I got to do to sort of like, completely focus on doing this.
objections.rep_response: Investigated it properly — asked what the Ladder contract looked like, learned it was around $100 a month and month-to-month with no minimum term, and concluded 'the contract seems easy'. Having established the blocker was trivial, he did not then convert it back into a close.

offer.guarantee_mentioned: Read aloud in full from the agreement on a shared screen, the most complete statement of it in this batch: 'we're going to add at least eight kilograms to their working weight on at least three of the following five core kettlebell lifts, that's going to be kettlebell swing, kettlebell [snatch], kettlebell clean, kettlebell press, and kettlebell thruster, has to be logged in true coach, here's the eligibility. So, you have to complete at least 90% of the prescribed workouts, submit the weekly form check-in with the grace of up to two missed check-ins per calendar quarter, maintain reasonable communication with the coach, provide accurate information regarding workout completion, there is permitted pauses if a life event comes up, but if you satisfy all the qualifying conditions and don't achieve that performance benchmark by the end of the program term, Trevor will actually coach you for free until you do.' Separately: 'if you complete, I think it's like 90% of the workouts... you get $500 credit towards renewal of coaching if you want to do that, okay? And there's usually a discount on it if you do want to stay in.'

evidence: No payment taken and no card given. The prospect declined at the point of collection: 'Amex, but I would love to see something a little bit more in writing before I give you my credit card.'
No verbal agreement to proceed. 'I wasn't prepared to sign on the bottom line today.'
What was sent was the coaching agreement for review, not a payment link, so the verbal-agreement-plus-link rule does not apply: 'All right, I'll fire it off... Okay, I just sent it to you right now.'

Counter-evidence, strongly positive: he rated the programme a 10 out of 10 against the best coach he has ever worked with, said 'this is, I think, what I would like to do', accepted $6,000 with no resistance at all, and told the rep money was 'really the last thing'.
Counter-evidence, negative: he stated plainly that continuing to use the free content forever remained an option — 'maybe that's what we'll end up doing' — and that was never addressed.
Follow-up is informal. 'And then I will reach out to you, I guess, on Monday' — the prospect owns the next action, no call was booked and no calendar hold was made.
outcome.next_step: Prospect to read the coaching agreement over the July 4th weekend and reach out on Monday 2026-07-06. Outstanding items on his side are reading the contract and cancelling a month-to-month Ladder subscription of roughly $100. He also raised, unresolved, that he will need to buy heavier kettlebells for his New York location.

notable.note: The most ICP-core prospect in this batch by a distance — sold a family business to Terminix, ex-Head of M&A, former PE portfolio CEO, fit, 59, no price resistance whatsoever — and he did not close, while a prospect with no established occupation who was managing a credit card limit closed at full price the same day. That contrast is the finding. Process-wise this was the rep's best discovery of the batch: real reflect-back, a genuine devil's-advocate challenge, and a full read of the contract on a shared screen when asked. It failed at the end for two avoidable reasons. First, the prospect said out loud that he could keep taking the free content forever and might do exactly that, and the rep did not respond. Second, having isolated the only remaining blockers as reading a contract and cancelling a $100 month-to-month app, the rep established both were trivial and then did not attempt to close again. Also unpriced: the prospect will need to buy heavier kettlebells to pursue the goal, raised by him and waved away with 'which is good'.

quality.notes: Continuous inversion, plus a device label. The prospect appears throughout as 'andrew's phone', and the labels are wrong more often than right — the rep's own pillar delivery, the $6,000 quote and most discovery questions sit under the prospect's label, while the prospect's answers sit under the rep's. Several long blocks contain both speakers with no break, notably the exchange at 00:10:49 where the rep's reflect-back and the prospect's agreement are fused into one turn. Roles resolved from content only.
